original_question: Consider Newton's equation u'' = -V'_u(u,t) with V periodic in both u and t. Besides the special case V = V(nu + mt), for which the system is known to be totally integrable near infinity, are there other potential functions V for which the system is totally integrable at infinity?
target_in_paper: Misha Bialy, Question 3 in the subsection on Newton equations with periodic potential: "Are there other potential functions such that the system is totally integrable at infinity?"
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the paper's intended target very closely: it uses the same time-periodic one-dimensional Newton equation, singles out the same known special family V(u,t)=W(nu+mt), and asks whether there are any other periodic potentials yielding total integrability at infinity.
missing_details: The paper frames the problem through the Euler-Lagrange equation for the Lagrangian L(u,\dot u,t)=\tfrac12\dot u^2-V(u,t), equivalently the Hamiltonian system with H(u,p,t)=\tfrac12 p^2+V(u,t).
The ambient periodicity is toric: u and t are periodic variables, so V is naturally viewed as a function on \mathbb T^2, not merely an unspecified periodic function on \mathbb R^2.
"Totally integrable at infinity" is not just "integrable for large energy"; in the section's terminology it means that a neighborhood of infinity is foliated by invariant graph tori.
The relevant neighborhood of infinity should be made explicit as a large-momentum region of the form \{|p|>C\} for some sufficiently large C.
The special known family should record that m and n are integers in the periodic ansatz nu+mt.
The paper explains why that family is known: it admits an additional first integral quadratic in the momentum p, implying total integrability near infinity.
The nearby context contrasts this open problem with the already-classified whole-phase-space case: total integrability on the whole phase space occurs if and only if V is independent of t.
Your draft leaves the regularity of V implicit; the paper simply says "periodic potential," so at least enough smoothness to define \partial_u V and the associated flow is being assumed.
refined_question: For the time-periodic Newton equation \ddot u=-\partial_u V(u,t), with V periodic in both u and t (equivalently V:\mathbb T^2\to\mathbb R), let H(u,p,t)=\tfrac12 p^2+V(u,t) be the associated Hamiltonian system on the extended phase space. Here "totally integrable at infinity" means that there exists C>0 such that the region \{|p|>C\} is foliated by invariant graph tori of the flow. Besides the known family V(u,t)=W(nu+mt) with m,n\in\mathbb Z, for which there is an additional first integral quadratic in p and hence total integrability in a neighborhood of infinity, are there any other periodic potentials V for which the system is totally integrable at infinity?
justification: The draft is targeting Misha Bialy's Question 3, not a broader neighboring problem. In the immediately preceding context, the paper first defines total integrability for toric configuration spaces as foliation by invariant graph tori, then specializes to the periodic Newton equation, states the whole-phase-space classification and the known family V=W(nu+mt) with a quadratic-in-momentum integral, and finally asks exactly whether there are other potentials giving total integrability at infinity. The refined version therefore keeps the scope unchanged while making the phase space, the momentum variable p, the large-momentum neighborhood \{|p|>C\}, and the meaning of "totally integrable at infinity" explicit.
